How to Read a Squall Line

The sky tells you nearly everything twenty minutes ahead. Here is how to listen.

DL
Dag Lindmark10 November 2026 · 7 min read

A squall line announces itself long before it arrives, if you know what you are looking at. First the horizon to windward darkens and hardens into a shelf. Then the sea under that shelf changes color, from blue-grey to a darker, rougher grey, as the wind reaches the water. That dark band moving toward you is the squall itself.

You usually have fifteen to twenty minutes from the first sight of the shelf. Use them. Reef early, close the hatches, put on the jacket you thought you would not need, and decide now which way you will bear away if the gusts are worse than expected.

Most squalls are over in ten minutes. The rain stops, the wind drops, and the sky behind the line is often the cleanest blue of the day. The trick is to be ready for the ten minutes, and to enjoy the hour after. ■
